Cash Caterpillar- Mopane Worms

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Masontja (Mopane worm)

While Dutch farmers face the mass culling of livestock because of an overload of nitrogen pollution, in Africa the humble mopane worm gives off less greenhouse gases and contains protein levels of 60%, higher than meat or fish.
Yet while we relish blood seeping steak, hideous looking prawns and crayfish that feed on effluent, we squirm at the thought of eating these nutritious caterpillars, which have been part of the African diet for centuries.
The Gonimbrasia Belina is a species of moth, native to Botswana, parts of the North West province, Limpopo, Zimbabwe and Namibia.
It feeds almost exclusively on the mopane tree and its offspring is slowly making its way onto mainstream menus.
This story will also look at the trade in mopane worms – from the tree to the plate – their sustainability (shrinking mopane forests) and carbon footprint (they need less space – 3 kg of mopani leaves equals 1kg of worms, while cattle farmers need 10 kg of feed to make 1kg of beef).

Locations:
Harvesting/cultivation in Limpopo/Venda or Botswana/North West
Journey to cities via traders
Street sellers
Online sellers
Manufacturers
Cooking & eating
Sustainability & carbon footprint

Characters:

Dr James Sekonya – did his PhD on the mopani worm trade – and found that the market was concentrated in urban areas and supplied by imports from Botswana and Zimbabwe, with most of the value going to traders, rather than harvesters. With villages expanding in Limpopo, mopane forests are being chopped down for fencing & firewood, increasing the reliance on worms from Botswana. Botswanan worms are bigger, being harvested when they reach a particular size, which means lots more meaty goodness and less leaf matter. To protect our wild population of worms in SA, commercial farming needs to be implemented and we need to learn from Zimbabwe & Botswana, he says. He’s willing to accompany a CB team to harvesting and trading sites in the Vhembe and Mopani districts of Limpopo in December, which is when they are harvested and transported to market. Or just across the border to Botswana, where availability is greater.
james.sekonya@mandela.ac.za
https://open.uct.ac.za/bitstream/handle/11427/36554/thesis_sci_2022_sekonya%20james%20george.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y
Wendy Vesela-Ntimbani – chemical engineer who grew up in Limpopo and learnt the art of harvesting worms with her parents in the mopani forests and is trying to ensure their sustainability in that part of the world:

Over the years there has been over-harvesting of the mopanes. We need to regenerate the population of the mopane worms to ensure the life cycle of the emperor moth continues, for future generations to enjoy what I’ve enjoyed.

She has a company called Matomane (Tsonga for mopani worm) that turns them into flour used in savoury biscuits, protein bars and cereals.

Her website says they are a cost-effective alternative to meat, fish & chicken – but her products look expensive. https://www.matomani.com/products/
Compare her price of unprocessed worms to price of meat per gram.
067 641 2139; info@matomani.com

Phuthi Kabasa calls herself the Mopane Bites Queen and turns mopani worms into ‘banting-friendly’ snacks like tortillas & crisps.

https://www.mopanibites.com/blog
063 802 4194
sales@mopanibites.com

Other interviews:
Dept of Agriculture about sustainability projects and plans – wild worms or worm farms? They had a project near Ganyesa in North West, but the moths disappeared, it’s believed to Namibia and Botswana, because of overexploitation.

Tito Mboweni: he’s been approached via Treasury with a view to cooking a worm meal for our presenter. He declined, but let’s not give up on him. Third hand messages can be misinterpreted.
https://briefly.co.za/80047-tito-mboweni-cooks-a-storm-mopane-worms-mzansi-reacts.html

Alternately, we could get a chef to prepare them for our presenter. They are on the menu of this Cape Town restaurant, along with crickets and ants.

https://www.independent.ie/life/food-drink/food-news/south-africans-get-the-bug-inside-the-cape-town-insect-restaurant-where-worms-termites-and-crickets-are-on-the-menu-38462093.html


Food sustainability expert:
Professor Sheryl Hendriks is a food security policy expert with extensive experience in policy analysis and programme design. She is engaged in high-level global food security policy think tanks and panels and is influential in food security and nutrition policy in Africa.
sheryl.hendriks@up.ac.za

Script:


Mopane Final Script


V/O

Obz or Observatory in Cape Town is a colourful mix of cafes, bars and pavement hangouts.

Tucked away, down a Harry Potter alley is a slim little ice cream shop that brews magic in cauldrons.

Up Sound - This looks really cool.

V/O
The philosopher wizard with the wooden spoon is Zimbabwean Tapiwa Guzha.

Up Sound “ I do everything by hand I am the machine here.”

V/O
Tapiwa’s special power is ice cream. The potions he’s perfected are to reach his true goal: Re-educating Africans about food and cultural beliefs.

Masa
This is going to be my first time tasting amasi flavoured ice cream

Tapiwa
Today is the day

Up Sound patrons
Sweet potato jam in tea ice cream. I’ll have the plum actually.

Link
At this ice cream store you will not find rum and raisin or choc chip. Here you will find flavours that challenge the taste buds using authentic African flavours.

V/O
Creations like imphepho smoke & Kalahari salt to clay ice cream.



Masa
How did we get to the flavours because it is not just any ice cream you have here?

Tapiwa
That happened by chance. I was in a restaurant in Salt river where they sell Zimbabwean food and I said I wonder what that would taste like if I put it into ice cream. Bought some fruit from the market and went home, Baobab and Masawu, made those first 5 flavours and that’s when I realised. All along I have been having ice cream in a very strange way.


V/O
A doctorate in molecular biology has helped Tapiwa create gastronomic fame with an unusual signature dish of…wait for it…mopane worm ice cream!

Masa tastes
Hmmmmm
Wow I kid you not

Tapiwa
The proudest moments in this space are when you get someone to change their mind, examine their prejudices and shift their internal bias system a little bit.

Masa Link
When I came here I had no idea what to expect. Now I don’t know how I am going to leave.

Masa Link
Ask anyone to name indigenous South African crops and they usually would be at a loss for words but with the climate crisis intensifying, underutilised and lesser-known crops are likely to become the superstars of food security.

Pause for thunder




V/O
Tracing the source of Tapiwa’s star ingredient, we travel to the border of the Kruger Park in Limpopo.

More thunder

Here spring rains bring the Southern African woodlands… and mopane trees to life… that feed and lend their name to the large edible caterpillar that hatches from the eggs laid by the emperor moth.

Joburg chemical engineer Wendy Vesela-Ntimbani comes home to Phalaborwa twice every year for the Christmas and Easter mopane worm harvest. It’s also precious family time with her father, Reckson.

Wendy
This is my dad, Mr Ntaimbani and my harvesting comes from him and my mother. I Caught up with him which is lovely and we have a bucket of big worms here.

V/O
Like most people here, who grow up eating mopane worms, the Ntimbani family harvests for household use and to generate income.

Wendy Father
It’s a nice game. Most of the people enjoy being in the bush like this.

Wendy
It’s a community as well. You are talking; you are having a good time and picking that delicacy.

V/O
Wendy believes mopanes are vastly under-rated, because unlike livestock, they thrive in the wild, without fertilisers, hormones or husbandry, and they have three times more protein than beef. And generate hardly any greenhouse gasses.

V/O
Some may find them too squeamish …these harvesters pity them

“I think they are scared of them”

Up Sound laughing

V/O
Taking the worms from the tree to the table is far easier than livestock. They are washed, boiled, dried in the sun and then they are good to go.

Wendy’s has left her chemical engineering career and started a mopane worm company.

Mopanes are becoming big business… estimated at over a billion rand just in Southern Africa… Wendy has created a number of products and reduced dried worms to a protein-rich flour.

Wendy
Protein powder… consumers are using it in their smoothies. They're using it for protein recovery and things like that.

Masa
Looking at African foods with the research you know that we are getting that we are realising more and more, their nutritional value and that they are environmentally sound?

Tapiwa
I think historically, if you look at it, people always knew what was good for them and what was good for the land.

V/O
Mosima Mabitsela who grew up in a small village near Polokwane says her family thrived on the worms.

Mosima
I love how we create a relish with them and then just eat them with pap. You don’t need meat. But some people don’t like them; they feel like we are eating bugs.

Masa
And yet they eat prawns.

Mosima
Yes, they are like these are indigenous prawns. No, those are mopane worms.

Up Sound Those are the insects that are causing the trouble.

V/O
Mosima is a PHD student in agriculture at the University of Stellenbosch. Back home she could see how global warming was hitting subsistence farmers like her father hard. Mamothatha Mabitsela’s non indigenous crops struggled without fertilisers and pesticides.

Up Sound These are the insects that are causing trouble.

Mosima
I want to be a researcher that can go out into communities and educate them about climate change and how they can adapt with the minimal resources that they have.

V/O
At the university, Mosima is experimenting with another indigenous crop of her youth.

Up Sound “I come here every day, 6 am I need to be here.

V/O
The Bambara nut was a childhood comfort food - and it turns out it’s an African supercrop. She’s testing how they fare in sawdust and mist…for future adverse conditions .

Mosima
It's a climate smart crop. It's heat resistant. For instance, temperatures can go up to 38 in the tunnel. That's extremely hot. But then it's giving me the yield that that's very, very good.

V/O

Mosima believes that the bambara nut may play a pivotal role to reduce South Africa’s dependence on environmentally risky mono crops like rice, wheat and maize.

Masa
And just from your experience what are some of the misconceptions that you have found about African food?

Part of it is that we are skeptical of blackness, anything made by an African has always got to be vetted and questioned so there is an underlying current of skepticism of anything any African does.

V/O
Tapiwa believes that we need to embrace African produce, like the mopane worm and bambara nuts,
with their nutritional and environmental benefits, they will play a pivotal role in the continents future food security. His ice cream he says, may just be the catalyst.

Tapiwa
I think ice cream is a nice analogue for the rest of life, we live on that continent and we should be enjoying most of this continent.

PROMO 1

VO:
It’s not everyone’s idea of a balanced meal, but the lowly mopane worm is taking center stage with gourmet dishes like ice-cream…

UPSOUND: Masa
I want a big piece. Hmmmm. I want more. MMM (LEAVE OUT TAPIWA LAUGH)

VO:
Meet the indigenous foods that are becoming part of a protein revolution…


PROMO 2
The climate crisis is forcing a change to focus on underutilized indigenous African crops.

Mosima:
It's a climate smart crop. It's heat resistant.

Wendy:
Edible insects contribute almost zero so people should be eating mopane worms rather than meat.

Meet 2 women trying to bring mopane worms and bambara nuts onto mainstream platters.

So what’s stopping us?

PROMO 3

Part-scientist, part-chef, Dr Tapiwa Guzha is on a mission to re-educate Africans about indigenous food. And he is achieving this through mopane worm ice cream.

metadata.Summary: Masontja (Mopane worm) While Dutch farmers face the mass culling of livestock because of an overload of nitrogen pollution, in Africa the humble mopane worm gives off less greenhouse gases and contains protein levels of 60%, higher than meat or fish. Yet while we relish blood seeping steak, hideous looking prawns and crayfish that feed on effluent, we squirm at the thought of eating these nutritious caterpillars, which have been part of the African diet for centuries. The Gonimbrasia Belina is a species of moth, native to Botswana, parts of the North West province, Limpopo, Zimbabwe and Namibia. It feeds almost exclusively on the mopane tree and its offspring is slowly making its way onto mainstream menus. This story will also look at the trade in mopane worms – from the tree to the plate – their sustainability (shrinking mopane forests) and carbon footprint (they need less space – 3 kg of mopani leaves equals 1kg of worms, while cattle farmers need 10 kg of feed to make 1kg of beef). Locations: Harvesting/cultivation in Limpopo/Venda or Botswana/North West Journey to cities via traders Street sellers Online sellers Manufacturers Cooking & eating Sustainability & carbon footprint Characters: Dr James Sekonya – did his PhD on the mopani worm trade – and found that the market was concentrated in urban areas and supplied by imports from Botswana and Zimbabwe, with most of the value going to traders, rather than harvesters. With villages expanding in Limpopo, mopane forests are being chopped down for fencing & firewood, increasing the reliance on worms from Botswana. Botswanan worms are bigger, being harvested when they reach a particular size, which means lots more meaty goodness and less leaf matter. To protect our wild population of worms in SA, commercial farming needs to be implemented and we need to learn from Zimbabwe & Botswana, he says.
